Carousel. The 1945 musical by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II, adapted from Ferenc Molnár's play Liliom. Set in a New England coastal town, it tells the tragic love story between Billy Bigelow, a rough carousel barker, and Julie Jordan, a textile mill worker, exploring themes of redemption, sacrifice, and the unending bond between parent and child even beyond death.

This was their second major collaboration after Oklahoma!, deepening the partnership further. The score includes the ballad duet "If I Loved You," establishing the central romance; the joyful ensemble number "June Is Bustin' Out All Over"; "Soliloquy," an eight-minute extended dramatic monologue where Billy reveals his interior struggle over fatherhood, shame, and desperation, culminating in his decision to commit suicide; and "You'll Never Walk Alone," the closing hymn. The Soliloquy stands as one of musical theatre's most challenging arias.

The show opened with an extended dance sequence rather than dialogue, choreography by Agnes de Mille establishing a visual vocabulary of character and emotion. The plot culminates in Billy's death during a robbery attempt, but then the musical extends into the afterlife. Billy is given a chance to return and help his daughter at a crucial moment, reframing the entire narrative as an act of love.

Carousel opened on Broadway in 1945 and ran for 890 performances. The 1956 film, also directed by Henry King, starred Gordon MacRae and Shirley Jones. It is often cited as the darkest and most emotionally profound of the Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals, with a protagonist who is neither wholly good nor wholly redeemable.
